description:
The Ten Commandments are presented as a continuing summary of moral law grounded in God’s character. After reviewing the distinction between moral, civil and ceremonial law, Wesam Saad turns to the new covenant promise that God will write his law on his people’s hearts. He argues that moral law carries over rather than being discarded. The command to love is then connected with the commandments through Paul’s teaching, Jesus’ summary of love for God and neighbour, and James’s account of the royal law. Saad also distinguishes the conscience described in Romans from the new heart given in regeneration.

The argument proceeds from the commandments’ authority to their distinctive presentation: spoken by God, written on stone, and described as his work. Saad relates the opening commands to God’s jealousy and holiness, and the Sabbath command to his act of creation. He treats these connections as reasons not to detach the fourth commandment from the rest. This session develops that case without yet resolving the later questions about Sunday worship or the practical limits of rest. The closing exchange deliberately leaves matters such as cooking and the number of working days for another discussion, keeping attention on whether the weekly holy day remains binding.

questions.question: How is the new covenant promise used to support continuing moral law?
questions.answer: Saad asks what Jeremiah’s first hearers would have understood by God’s promise to write his law on their hearts. He argues that this points to moral law rather than civil or ceremonial regulations. The promise is therefore used in his case for continuity, not for replacing all earlier moral obligation with an unrelated code.

questions.question: Does the command to love replace the Ten Commandments in this exposition?
questions.answer: No. Saad treats love for God and neighbour as the summary of what the commandments require. He draws on Paul’s examples, Jesus’ twofold summary and James’s royal-law passage to argue that love and moral commands belong together. The commandments explain the shape of obedience rather than competing with love.

questions.question: How does he answer the objection that some passages mention only duties towards neighbours?
questions.answer: He agrees that passages about loving neighbours naturally cite duties towards other people. He then relates that section to the corresponding duties towards God and later points to Paul’s discussion of idolatry in Romans. His argument treats the commandments as a connected whole, rather than inferring that an unquoted command has been cancelled.

questions.question: What distinction is made between conscience and the new heart?
questions.answer: When reading Romans 2, Saad expressly says that the law’s witness in Gentile consciences is not the new heart received in regeneration. He follows Paul’s discussion into the commands against theft, adultery and idolatry to identify the moral standard being considered. He does not make a person’s subjective feeling of guilt the final standard.

questions.question: Why does the command to honour parents matter to the wider argument?
questions.answer: Saad focuses on Paul’s description of it as the first commandment with a promise. He understands that wording as referring to the recognised set of Ten Commandments and therefore as acknowledging that set’s authority. This is a step in his argument for retaining the fourth commandment with the others, rather than a separate treatment of parenting.

questions.question: What significance does Saad give to the commandments’ presentation at Sinai?
questions.answer: He stresses their direct proclamation by God, their inscription on stone and the description of the tablets as God’s work. He reads this distinctive presentation as showing their importance. The point leads into his claim that they reveal God’s character, rather than merely being a convenient list of ancient social rules.

questions.question: How are the opening commandments connected with God’s character and acts?
questions.answer: Saad connects the rejection of other gods and idols with God’s jealousy, reverence for his name with holiness, and the Sabbath with creation. He argues that these foundations are not limited to Israel’s later covenant arrangements. The connection is part of his case for the continuing moral significance of the fourth commandment.

questions.question: Which questions about Sabbath observance remain open at this stage?
questions.answer: The session has not yet worked through why the church gathers on Sunday or what particular activities fit the day. Questions about cooking and the number of working days are explicitly set aside. Saad identifies the present task as establishing whether one day each week should be kept holy before discussing those implications.
